newsitem.title: USA: U.S. refiners keeping watch on Colombian strike.
newsitem.headline: U.S. refiners keeping watch on Colombian strike.

text.p: Some major U.S. Gulf Coast refiners, accustommed to a steady diet of sweet Cusiana and other Colombian grades, are keeping watch on the progress of the country's ongoing public-sector strike.
Several spot Cusiana cargoes are due on the Gulf Coast in March, and so far refiners sound confident that the contracts will be met.

"I'm not worried--yet," said one regular U.S. buyer who is waiting on two Cusiana cargoes loading March 8-13 and March 17-21 from state-owned Ecopetrol. "I haven't seen anything to make me worry yet."

A U.S. domestic refiner, which recently agreed with a major broker to exchange a North Sea Brent cargo for March 5-10 delivery for a Cusiana cargo, echoed that confidence. "There are always problems in Colombia, there's always concern," a company official said. "But I think the oil will get out."
A European equity producer in Colombia sounded a more cautious note. "There's no impact into the loading programs expected, but that could change," he said.
Another European equity producer noted that previous Colombian strikes had actually expanded market availabilities because local refineries were not running at full capacity.
The walkout has cut gasoline production at the Barrancabermeja refinery by 15 percent, but crude output, pumping operations and exports have not been affected, an Ecopetrol spokesman said on Tuesday.
But the head of the USO, Hernando Hernandez, contended that production, refining and pumping have been cut by 50 percent.
Meanwhile, the country's leftist guerrillas have thrown their weight behind the strike, threatening "expressions of violence" and "grassroots disobedience."

A spokesman for U.S. equity producer Occidental Petroleum Corp indicated that field activities were normal. "Production and transaportation are unaffected by the strike, and some (of the company's) workers showed an increased willingness to work."
An estimated 800,000 public-sector workers, including members of the 7,000-strong USO oil workers' union, began an indefinite strike at midnight Monday (0500 GMT Tuesday) to demand higher pay.
